# Summary: Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer engineer whose life was shaped by both wartime experience and post-war technological ambition. Born in Turin, Italy to a family of noted alpinists and intellectuals, Karpiński suffered major injuries during World War II while a member of the Polish resistance, yet went on to overcome physical challenges and excel academically. His early career included work on ultrasonography under Leszek Filipkowski, and the creation of the Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics (AAH), a vacuum tube computer used to improve long-term weather forecasts. His collaboration on AKAT-1 (1959), the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer, brought him international acclaim and a UNESCO engineering scholarship in the United States, where he collected intelligence for Polish authorities.
Karpiński's most significant achievements include the KAR-65 computer (1968)—the fastest Polish computer of its time, and the innovative minicomputer K-202 (1971–73), which surpassed many Western competitors yet failed to reach mass production due to political, economic, and institutional barriers in communist Poland. His career was marred by persistent state interference, censorship, and controversy surrounding his role as a secret informant, as well as debates over the true impact and originality of his creations. After his engineering career waned, Karpiński spent years in Switzerland and rural Poland, later advising government officials and attempting various business ventures. He received notable honors (including the Officer's and Commander's Crosses of Polonia Restituta) and remains a debated and symbolic figure in the history of Polish computer science.
